fixes.explanation: Yes, his nurse. Jehosheba, King Joram's daughter and Ahaziah's sister, takes Joash and puts him and his nurse in a bedroom. The text says she did it to hide him from Athaliah, Ahaziah's mother. I think this one is heavy, with the king's sons being murdered all around. But the verse ends with “…and he was not killed.” (2 Kings 11:2)

Not his mother, friend. The text says Jehosheba stole Joash away from among the sons of the king who were being murdered. Then she put him and his nurse in a bedroom to hide him from Athaliah. So the one with him in that room is his nurse.

That's it. Joash remained hidden with his nurse in the house of the LORD for six years while Athaliah ruled the land. Six years is a long time to stay tucked away. The text puts him right there in the house of the LORD.
Not a palace, friend. The text says Joash remained hidden with his nurse in the house of the LORD. That's where they stay for six years while Athaliah rules the land.

Yes! Jehoiada the priest shows the commanders the king's son, and that's Joash, Ahaziah's little boy. He does it after making a covenant with them and putting them under oath. After six years of Joash staying hidden, those commanders get to see him. I bet they had a lot to think about in that moment.
Jehu isn't in this room, friend. After the covenant and the oath, Jehoiada the priest shows the commanders the king's son. That's Joash, Ahaziah's little boy, the one who's been hidden away.
No questions first. The order is that anyone who approaches the ranks must be put to death. Jehoiada has the guards surround the king with weapons in hand. I think this is a heavy order.

Not sent home. Jehoiada's order in verse 8 is that anyone who approaches the ranks must be put to death. The guards are surrounding the king with weapons in hand. I think this is a heavy order, and it shows how seriously he wants the king protected.
True. Jehoiada says, “You must stay close to the king wherever he goes.” (2 Kings 11:8) That's an order to surround him with weapons in hand. Where Joash goes, the guards stay close.

David it is. Jehoiada gives the commanders the spears and shields of King David from the house of the LORD. Those weapons were in the house of the LORD, and now they go to the commanders. Jehoiada the priest is the one handing them out.

Saul isn't named here. The text says Jehoiada gives the commanders the spears and shields of King David from the house of the LORD. Those are David's, not Saul's. Saul isn't mentioned in this passage.

Solomon is a good guess, since he was David's son. He took his seat on his father David's throne (1 Kings 2:12). But in this passage, Jehoiada is the one who gives the commanders the spears and shields of King David. They're David's, and Solomon isn't mentioned here.

A ring is a fair thing to picture with a king, but this verse doesn't mention one. Jehoiada brings out the king's son and puts the crown on him. Then he presents him with the Testimony and proclaims him king.

The new king, yes. Athaliah looks out and sees the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom. That's Joash, the one crowned in the house of the LORD. I think this is a rough moment for her.

Elisha isn't in this scene. When Athaliah looks out, the text says she sees the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom. The officers and trumpeters are beside the king. That king is Joash.

Jehu isn't the one standing there. Athaliah sees the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom. That's Joash, with the officers and trumpeters beside him. Jehu isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage.

She doesn't scream that word. Athaliah tears her clothes and screams, “Treason! Treason!” (2 Kings 11:14) She sees the king, the officers and trumpeters beside him, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets. That's what she's looking at when the word comes out.
Idols, yes. The people of the land go to the temple of Baal and tear it down. They smash the altars and idols to pieces. I bet that made some noise.
Lampstands aren't named in the text. The people tear down the temple of Baal, and they smash the altars and idols to pieces. So the altars and the idols are what the verse names.
No scrolls named here, friend. The people of the land tear down the temple of Baal and smash the altars and idols to pieces. Idols are what the text pairs with the altars in that list.

A chariot would be quite the ride, but the text doesn't mention one. They bring the king down from the house of the LORD and enter the royal palace by way of the Gate of the Guards. Then Joash takes his seat on the royal throne. That's the seat the verse names.
Seven, yes. The text says, “Joash was seven years old when he became king.” (2 Kings 11:21) Before this, he spent six years hidden with his nurse in the house of the LORD. Now he takes the throne.
